stories.title: Census 2027: Assam begins 2nd phase amid flood delays, border tensions
stories.summary: The March 31, 2027, deadline looms as Assam grapples with flood-hit districts and resistance to enumeration along disputed borders
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma announced that the state government has successfully identified 57,000 families eligible for flood compensation across the worst-hit eastern districts.
The state machinery completed a series of comprehensive, door-to-door field surveys to ensure no genuine victim is left out of the rehabilitation drive.

Speaking to reporters, the Chief Minister confirmed that verified survey data detailing the extensive infrastructural and property damages in three key districts will be dispatched to the Central Government within the next two days.
The state expects a swift release of central funds to bolster ongoing financial aid distribution.
The announcement comes amidst escalating political friction in the state.
Opposition Raijor Dal MLA Akhil Gogoi has been staging an indefinite sit-in on the Assembly premises, demanding enhanced relief payouts of ₹10 lakh per family.

Dismissing the protests as "politically motivated," Sarma countered that families have already been systematically informed of their exact direct benefit transfer (DBT) entitlements based on scientific damage assessments.

The state government, which previously rolled out initial relief packages of ₹15,000 per household to nearly one lakh families, remains committed to fully restoring damaged properties and livelihoods.

stories.title: Monocracy In Election Commission: Testing Statutory Consensus Under 2023 CEC Act
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: A Public Interest Litigation filed in the Supreme Court on September 25, 2026, by advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi has brought an unprecedented internal rift within the Election Commission of India into the judicial spotlight.

It seeks the initiation of criminal proceedings against the Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, under Section 32 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, as well as a probe into the alleged unilateral orders of the CEC by forming a Special Investigation Team.

As per Indian Express expose, fourteen formal written objections to the Chief Election Commissioner's executive orders by the Election Commissioners Dr. Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Dr. Vivek Joshi were documented over a period of ten months, which cannot be dismissed as routine administrative friction.

The internal breach regarding the Chief Election Commissioner's unilateral executive orders without collective decision-making, the modification of voter registration rules via updates to digital portals, and the centralization of electoral rolls management in Delhi represent direct violations of multi-member decision-making obligations per the Representation of the People Act, 1950 and the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.

The Election Commission's official defense, issued on September 23, 2026, and reiterated following an all-member meeting on September 26, 2026, that written notes merely reflect standard internal deliberation fails statutory scrutiny.
In T.N. Seshan.

Union of India, the Supreme Court unambiguously denied the possibility of the existence of a supreme Chief Election Commissioner, as the statutory scheme was purposefully devised to prevent arbitrary executive governance.
The violation of this results in transforming the internal dispute into administrative illegality.
Multi-Member Governance or Monocratic Rule?
The statutory framework governing the internal decision-making process is established in Section 18 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023.
Per Section 18(2), the Commission shall transact its business unanimously.
Where there is a difference of opinion between the Chief Election Commissioner and the other Election Commissioners, then the matter will be decided according to the opinion of the majority.

article_sentences: Congress workers staged a protest rally in Hubballi on October 11, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of electoral malpractice and attempts to undermine democracy.

The rally was organised by the Vidyanagar and Unkal block Congress committees under the leadership of Rajat Ullagaddimath, Chairperson of the Hubballi-Dharwad City District Guarantee Schemes Implementation Authority.
It began at Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Circle, where the protesters read out Article 326 of the Constitution, which provides for elections based on adult suffrage.
Addressing the gathering, Mr. Ullagaddimath alleged that the RSS is conspiring to deprive oppressed and marginalised communities of their right to vote.
Describing the struggle to protect democracy and the Constitution as a ‘second freedom struggle’ against what he termed fascist forces, he called for concerted action to safeguard electoral rights.

Hundreds of Congress workers accused the BJP-led Union Government of attempting to manipulate the votes of Other Backward Classes, Economically Weaker Sections, Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and minority communities.
They raised slogans against the Centre and demanded Mr. Kumar’s resignation.
Tension prevailed when the rally reached the Hubballi-Dharwad Municipal Corporation office.
Protesters allegedly attempted to burn portraits of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union Home Minister Amit Shah, and Mr. Kumar, triggering a scuffle between the police and the demonstrators.
The police, subsequently, detained several protesters.

Hubballi-Dharwad District Congress president Sadanand Danganavar, I.G. Sanadi, KPCC member Satish Meharwade, Shahzaman Mujahid, Anwar Mudgol, Mohammed Sharif Gargad, and several councillors and party functionaries participated in the protest.

stories.title: Neither approved nor rejected ECI's new Form 6, clarifies Supreme Court
stories.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday clarified that it had not adjudicated on the Election Commission of India’s (ECI) modified Form 6 declaration for new voter registration, observing that the revised form was not before it when it decided the Bihar Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls case.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Monday clarified that it had not adjudicated on the Election Commission of India’s (ECI) modified Form 6 declaration for new voter registration, observing that the revised form was not before it when it decided the Bihar Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls case.

New Delhi: The Supreme Court on Monday clarified that it had not adjudicated on the Election Commission of India’s (ECI) modified Form 6 declaration for new voter registration, observing that the revised form was not before it when it decided the Bihar Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls case.

A bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana made the clarification while hearing a fresh petition raising concerns over the functioning of the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and the changes to Form 6, which requires applicants seeking registration as new voters to disclose whether they or their parents were mapped in the previous SIR.

During the hearing, counsel for the petitioner submitted that the Supreme Court had clarified on October 5 that the modified Form 6 had not been approved by it, while the ECI had claimed that the revised declaration had received the top court’s approval.

Responding to the submission, Justice Bagchi said the Supreme Court had not adjudicated on the new Form 6, adding that the revised form was not in existence when the judgment in the Bihar SIR case was delivered.
"There is no adjudication on the new Form 6," he observed, clarifying that the apex court’s earlier oral remarks could not be construed as either approving or disapproving the modified declaration.
CJI Surya Kant cautioned against selectively interpreting the top court’s observations for media reports, saying: "Please don’t pick words for news items."

The clarification comes amid a political row over the modified Form 6 declaration, with questions being raised about the circumstances in which the changes were introduced and whether they were implemented despite objections from two Election Commissioners.

The controversy intensified after the ECI issued a press release on September 26 suggesting that the Supreme Court had upheld the revised declaration in its May 2026 judgment concerning the Bihar SIR exercise.
However, the modified declaration was introduced after the judgment, and the Supreme Court had no occasion to examine its contents while deciding the Bihar SIR matter.
Under the revised declaration, applicants seeking registration as new voters are required to state whether they or their parents were included in the previous SIR.
The earlier version of Form 6 used during the SIR exercise in other states did not contain this requirement.

The Congress leader has called on the “youth, all opposition parties, civil society groups, all those who believe in democracy and stand by the Constitution of India” to join the march.

The Supreme Court on Monday said there was a need to balance religious sentiments with public health concerns while considering restrictions on firecrackers in Delhi-NCR.

Hearing a suo motu matter on air pollution in the National Capital Region, the court said people should voluntarily shift to less polluting ways of celebrating festivals instead of depending only on restrictive judicial orders.

A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said it was not inclined to hurt religious sentiments, but stressed that citizens must be made aware of the harmful effects of firecrackers and encouraged to adopt safer practices.

"We will not hurt religious sentiments but at the same time, people should themselves come forward and opt for it.
The whole exercise should involve a balancing approach," the CJI said.
He added that awareness among citizens and civil society would be the most effective way forward.
During the hearing, Justice Bagchi questioned the religious basis for bursting firecrackers, asking, "What is religious about bursting crackers?"
Senior advocate Aparajita Singh, assisting the bench as amicus curiae, referred to the health risks of air pollution, especially for children, elderly people and those with health vulnerabilities.

Responding to arguments linking firecrackers with religious practices, she said, "Gods would be aghast if they knew that children were suffering and getting sick in their name." She also pointed to repeated enforcement failures, saying restrictions on the duration of firecracker use were unlikely to work without proper implementation.

From the selected films, the jury will recommend three films for the main competition, two films for the Best Debut Film of a Director category, and three films for the ICFT UNESCO-Gandhi Medal under the international competition. The jury will also evaluate entries for the Best Debut Director of Indian Feature Film Award, recommending five films and selecting the winner. The primary jury screening of eligible feature film entries commenced online on September 29 and is scheduled to continue until October 16, 2026. This will be followed by the central panel jury screening of 60 shortlisted feature films at the NFDC Auditorium in Mumbai from October 18 to November 1, 2026. article_sentences: The Supreme Court was on Monday urged to urgently list contempt petitions alleging violation of its 2024 judgment on genetically modified (GM) crops, amid concerns over the alleged approval for the cultivation of herbicide-tolerant GM basmati rice.

A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana was told by lawyer Prashant Bhushan that now, the approval for cultivation of herbicide-tolerant GM basmati rice has been given and hence the contempt plea be heard as early as possible.
The lawyer referred to the 2024 judgment delivered by a bench of Justices B V Nagarathna and Sanjay Karol, which had a split verdict on one issue that was referred to a larger bench.
He said the contempt petitions arose from the common judgment and were unrelated to the reference concerning GM mustard, which was listed before a special three-judge bench.
"The contempt petitions are not related to the reference.
They arise out of the common judgment of the court.
They can be listed before the regular contempt bench," Bhushan submitted.
He said the contempt petition, filed in 2025, had not been taken up despite being mentioned earlier.
According to him, the special bench hearing the GM mustard reference had declined to hear the contempt petitions.
"They have now given the go-ahead to plant genetically modified basmati rice, which is a herbicide-tolerant variety.
It will destroy our basmati.

A bench of Justice MM Sundresh and Justice Prasanna B Varale issued notice on the petition filed by the Punjab government challenging the High Court's direction to register an FIR in the matter.

Senior Advocate Vikas Singh appeared for the State.

The case relates to alleged bribes paid to influence government transfers and postings, tenders, policy decisions, licensing and land-related matters.
The CBI registered the FIR on October 5, 2026, following a direction from the Punjab and Haryana High Court.

stories.title: N-E monsoon in sight as IMD predicts heavy rain for TN, Kerala, Karnataka, Coastal AP
stories.summary: Super El Nino raises stakes for 2026 north-east monsoon even as scientists note seasonal rainfall during El Nino years since 1976 have trended to be higher than during 1950-1976 period
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Conditions are turning favourable for the south-west monsoon to retreat from remaining parts of the country and the north-east monsoon to set in over the South Peninsula in the next 2-3 days.
Rainfall is expected to gather pace towards the weekend and around October 15 (Thursday), setting the stage for the seasonal transition.
With the onset of the north-east monsoon, the South Peninsula is likely to see a prolonged wet spell over the next 5–6 days.
India Meteorological Department (IMD) said.
Isolated heavy rainfall is expected over Kerala and Mahe, Coastal and South Interior Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal, and Coastal Andhra Pradesh.

The performance of the 2026 north-east monsoon will be closely watched against the backdrop of a potentially dominant super El Niño in the equatorial and eastern Pacific, touted as the strongest since 1950.
Historical studies suggest that north-east monsoon rainfall during El Niño years after 1976 was, on average, considerably higher than during the 1950–1976 period.

Scientists have pointed to changes in atmospheric circulation during El Niño that can strengthen easterly flows, transport more moisture towards the subcontinent and enhance rainfall over the South Peninsula.
Whether this historical relationship translates into a more generous north-east monsoon in 2026 remains to be seen.

For now, the retreating south-west monsoon, the emerging Bay of Bengal low-pressure area, and the prospect of intensifying rainfall across the South Peninsula make the next few days a critical watch period.
The IMD sees isolated heavy rainfall for Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal, Kerala and Mahe, and South Interior Karnataka for four days from Thursday.
Coastal Karnataka is likely to receive heavy rain on Saturday and Sunday, while North Interior Karnataka faces rain for three days from Friday.

stories.headline: Turning interest into fandom is our goal for women’s football: Jinisha Sharma
stories.title: Turning interest into fandom is our goal for women’s football: Jinisha Sharma
stories.summary: Of all the shenanigans Rebecca Welton pulls off in Ted Lasso, the much-feted American TV series about the fictional English football club AFC Richmond, nothing compares to her audacious bet in the recently concluded final season: Launching a women’s team against conventional wisdom and financial prudence. Jinisha Sharma, director of Capri Sports, the sports development arm of NBFC Capri Global, has watched the series too and knows all too well that the task she has taken on will require far more guts and gusto than Welton’s.Last month, Capri Sports, which also owns the franchise UP Warriorz (UPW) in the Women’s Premier League (WPL), signed a 15-year contract with the All India Football Federation (AIFF) to market and commercially develop the top two tiers of India’s national women’s football league—the Indian Women’s League (IWL) and IWL 2. Why has Capri chosen to invest in the women’s game, which has little visibility and following in the country? Sharma explains in a conversation with Forbes India. Edited excerpts:Q. Fifteen years is a long commitment in a sport that hasn’t yet had much commercial success. What convinced you to take the bet?At Capri Sports, we have been talking a lot about investing in women's sports. The contours of that include both where that is going to lead to a podium finish as well as where that is going to lead to commercial prowess. We have been evaluating multiple opportunities for quite some time to see where we can have a long-term impact, and women’s football has been on our mind from the very early days. This isn’t a decision we have taken just today, but years ago, when we started to evaluate which sports are primed for commercial success.Q. But women’s football doesn’t quite have that visibility yet.In sports, especially in women's sports, the connection needs to come from the audience. And we're hoping to bring in more young girls and women who become sports fans.One of the most important aspects of that continues to be their personal relationship with the sport. Our country has an incredible number of schools that offer an opportunity to play football, which means a lot of young girls have been exposed to football. In pop culture, too, they have consumed enough and more stories about the sport. Our bet has been based on our understanding of how we will be able to convert that association with a sport into its fandom. We are hoping IWL will be the missing link where girls who play football will also be able to watch it.We have seen that arc with the UP Warriorz (UPW) in the Women’s Premier League (WPL), where young girls and women are now starting to connect to cricket more deeply. We think this journey will be faster in football because a large number of young girls are into football already.And our investment in women’s football doesn’t start with the IWL. We have two initiatives prior to that—Warriorz FC, a senior district-level football team that Capri Sports owns in Mumbai, and Nova Sports, a football development pathway for girls.Also Read: How Jinisha Sharma is leading the charge for women's sports through WPLQ. But converting fandom might not automatically make a sports property a successful business. We have seen that with men’s football, which has an enormous following in India.Which is exactly why we have made the 15-year bet. We know there is a lot to do. None of us is saying that everything that we're imagining will happen right from the get-go. But we're hoping that bringing in a platform like this will enable more structure within women's football and lead to bigger moments. We've seen that, with far lesser investment and visibility, a far greater attempt at qualification at the AFC level is possible. So we see a lot of opportunity to drive commercial success with this. Apart from the WPL, we really feel football is another sport that can capture large audiences with a healthy female ratio.Q. Earlier, you spoke about how you have been evaluating this proposition for quite some time. What have you seen through that evaluation?One of the early markers for us, of course, was our journey with Warriorz FC, a senior district-level football team that Capri Sports owns in Mumbai. It helped us understand what the realities of women’s football are. We are not going into this doe-eyed and unaware of the challenges.One of the early things we have uncovered is that there is a lot of talent and a lot of interest among girls in playing. Between June 2022 and March 2024, the number of registered women footballers jumped from 11,724 to 27,936—that’s over 138 percent. But there is no clear pathway. If a girl starts playing football at eight, nine or ten, where does she go after that? Plus, there is a lack of access to structured training and consistent competition. So you don’t know where the long-term opportunities are. Warriorz FC gave us an understanding of what we need to solve for.Q. India is now a land of leagues. What do some of these leagues teach you about building another from scratch?Looking at both leagues that have done well and those that haven’t has helped us understand unit economics—how we need to invest the right amount and not overspend. Some of the early conversations we had with advisors who have worked on crafting leagues globally told us not to overinflate the proposition—let’s not try to position the league as the best ever, so don’t overpackage. While these are the two topmost tiers of women’s football, there are still realities like the quality of the grounds that they play on and the fact that clubs are still struggling, etc. We are hoping that the league will be able to grow gradually in such a manner that it will create recognition in the market and a connection with the audience.At the moment, we are focusing on making sure we produce it well so that the audience watching it for the first time will want to invest more time in the subsequent edition. We are debating whether we should refrain from going too wide in the funnel and making it a mass property. Is it more important to make the game more accessible or to build commercial value from Day 1—an example would be whether you want to put it behind a paywall?And most importantly, we need to build the storytelling through clubs, players and rivalries. The IWL started in 2016, but few people know about it. We will share whatever resources we have to help the clubs understand what to make of this opportunity. Most IWL club owners come from a place of passion, and we respect that deeply. We have to ensure this is now seen from the lens of growth as well.Also Read: How sports fandom helps build stronger professional relationshipsQ. Any templates from successful women’s leagues globally that you are looking to follow?There are two that we always speak about internally—the WSL in the UK and the NWSL in the US. They have given us a really good blueprint in the way they invest in match-day rituals to build fans. These are largely things that the clubs have done, but there are definitely learnings at a league level. We are here for 15 years, so we have to invest in the people. You just saw the passion for the game during the recent India-Brazil [friendly]. That needs to be tapped into. And, for that, the biggest thing that we have to do right now is build awareness. For instance, there are three clubs from Delhi in this year’s IWL—how incredible would it be to involve the city’s community and encourage some soccer rivalry?Internally, our discussion today isn’t about making it the biggest viewership property from day one. I want to make sure that I'm getting depth from the people who already care about football.And a lot of our conversations with fans have shown us that it’s got nothing to do with male or female fans—they just care about the game. Our conversations with fans have shown us that they care about the game, regardless of gender. So, our markers have shown that there is a lot of interest; now it's really our job to make sure that it sustains and then converts into fandom.Q. So, where do you start? What’s the first thing on your agenda?IWL 2 is really right upon us—it’s starting later this month. We've not really had much time with that. I am just focused on making sure that we're able to get all the systems in place for that. For IWL, of course, we are looking to ensure that the process to build the fan base gets started.

stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 12 : Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah on Monday said environmental protection cannot be the government's responsibility alone and called for collective public participation, even as he cautioned against any abrupt curbs on tourism that sustains thousands of families in the region. Speaking at the J&K Agriculture Science Congress 2026 at Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology of Kashmir (SKUAST-K), CM Omar Abdullah said the Union Territory was already facing the consequences of climate change, marked by erratic snowfall, water scarcity, landslides and floods. He said snowfall has become increasingly irregular, with insufficient winter precipitation hitting water availability in the following months. People face shortages in March, April and May, he said, only to see heavy rain and rising river levels later, triggering flood and landslide risks. This is our new reality. This is the reality we are living with," CM Omar said, stressing the need to sustain livelihoods while pursuing development. The Chief Minister said climate change cannot be fought by any single region or country in isolation and demands coordinated global action, while local communities must own the responsibility of protecting their surroundings and natural resources. On tourism, CM Omar said its environmental footprint must be addressed without disregarding the livelihoods of those dependent on the sector. He warned against suddenly restricting tourist arrivals, noting that tourism is the mainstay of many local families and businesses, and said any regulation of visitor numbers would have to be gradual and balanced. While conceding that tourism exerts pressure on the environment, he said tourists and vehicles alone cannot be blamed for pollution, plastic waste and water scarcity. He asked whether areas with negligible tourist activity were free of garbage and plastic pollution, and urged residents to look inward at their own practices. CM Omar came down heavily on the habit of throwing waste from vehicles and public transport, saying citizens must stop littering and take greater ownership of keeping their surroundings clean. He also urged people to cut down on single-use plastic bags by carrying reusable bags while shopping. Underlining the need for resource conservation, he asked people to avoid wasting water and to switch off lights, fans and heaters when not in use. The Chief Minister said that while the government has the primary responsibility for environmental protection, real change will come only through active public participation, and that sustainability and conservation can be achieved only when official action is matched by responsible citizen behaviour. (KNS).
